explanations: There is no defect. Each risky-looking spot is handled for its own context: the one f-string in the SQL interpolates only a value looked up in the fixed ORDER_BY dict, keyed by a Literal-validated field; the LIKE term is both bound as a parameter and escaped for wildcards with a matching ESCAPE clause; notes are escaped with html.escape at output time; uploaded names are discarded in favour of a random name plus an allow-listed suffix, with a resolve-and-contain check as a second layer; and CSV cells that start with formula characters are neutralized. Cuisine is checked with fullmatch, so no trailing-character loophole exists.

Parameter binding keeps the value out of the SQL text, which is what prevents injection. It does not change how LIKE interprets % and _ inside the value, so a user could match everything or enumerate names. like_contains prefixes those characters (and the backslash itself) with a backslash, and ESCAPE '\' tells SQLite that backslash is the escape character. It has nothing to do with case folding or encoding.

Identifiers and sort directions cannot be bound as parameters, so a lookup table is the standard approach. RestaurantQuery.sort is a Literal of three names, requests with other values are rejected by validation, and even then ORDER_BY[query.sort] yields a developer-written fragment. The other statements are false: the sort field is not passed through clean_text, ordering of the clauses is irrelevant, and SQLite would execute injected text in ORDER BY.

Encoding depends on where data is going: HTML needs entity escaping, CSV opened in a spreadsheet needs a formula guard, and a JSON API needs neither. Doing it at each output keeps stored data faithful and avoids double-escaping. clean_text normalizes Unicode and drops control and format characters but does not remove angle brackets, and authentication says nothing about the content of a note.
